From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American sculptor

For those of a similar name, see [Stephen Whyte (disambiguation)](link_0).

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/DublinBestClays.jpg/330px-DublinBestClays.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DublinBestClays.jpg)

Whyte with his sculptures of Dublin Soldiers (2019)

**Steven Whyte** (born 17 March 1969) is a sculptor classically trained in the traditional methodology of figurative [bronze](link_1) and portrait sculpture living in [Carmel, California](link_2). He has produced many public memorials and installations in both England and throughout the United States with subjects ranging from miners, to soldiers and fire fighters. He is credited with over fifty life size and larger bronze public figures and major monuments including _The Silverdale Mining Memorial_, _The Lance Sergeant [Jack Baskeyfield](link_3) VC Tribute_, _The Spirit of 1948_, and _The Dr. John Roberts Monument_. Whyte's multimillion-dollar, sixteen-figure monument in [San Diego](link_4), California entitled _National Salute to [Bob Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob\_Hope "Bob Hope") and the Military_ is one of his most notable works.

In 2010, Whyte unveiled a twice life size portrait monument of the 1957 [Heisman Trophy](link_5) Winner, [John David Crow](link_6) at [Texas A&M University](link_7) in [College Station, Texas](link_8), and a life-size full-relief statue of St. Anthony and Child at Basilica of [Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo](link_9) (Carmel Mission) [Carmel-by-the-Sea](link_10), California.

Whyte's work also includes four life-size figures for a memorial to the fallen officers of the San Diego Sheriff's Department which was unveiled in May 2011. He also completed a nine figure composition for [Cannery Row](link_11), [Monterey](link_12), CA, and a life size [Jumbo](link_13) the Elephant for [Tufts University](link_14), MA. One of Whyte's most complex works, the massive statue for [Texas A&M University](link_7) titled **The [Aggie War Hymn](link_15) Monument**, has twelve 1.6 times life size bronze figures of students, "sawing off varsity's horns". The 10 ft by 39 ft sculpture was unveiled in September 2014, at a cost of $1.7M. In 2016 Whyte was awarded Sports Artist of the Year, sculptor, by The [United States Sports Academy](link_16) and The American Sport Art Museum & Archives.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Whyte#cite_note-1) In December 2016 The [Smithsonian Institution](link_17) acquired Whyte's bronze bust of Congressman [John Conyers](link_18) Jr. for the [National Portrait Gallery (United States)](link_19) in Washington D.C..

Whyte was the sculptor for the Column of Strength, San Francisco's controversial [Comfort Women](link_20) Memorial.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steven_Whyte&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

**Steven Whyte** is a British-American figurative sculptor known for his classically inspired public monuments and portraiture. With a career spanning over 30 years, he has created more than 80 life-size or larger public bronze figures installed globally. Based in Carmel, California, Whyte is a Fellow of the [National Sculpture Society](link_21) and a former vice president of the Royal Society of Portrait Sculptors. His work is featured in the collections of the Smithsonian Institution and the Carter Presidential Library.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steven_Whyte&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Whyte was born in England. He was the only undergraduate ever accepted into the prestigious Sir Henry [Dalton School](link_22) of Sculpture, where he studied under Dame Elizabeth Fink RA and Professor [Colin Melbourne](link_23) ARCA. Before graduating, he began receiving high-profile portrait commissions, including [Keith Sutton](link_24) ([Bishop of Lichfield](link_25)), Viscount Blakenham, the Earl of Stockton, Sir John Harvey-Jones, and the Speaker of the House of Commons.

Disturbed by the decline of figurative sculpture in formal education, Whyte co-created the first nationally validated course devoted to figurative sculpture with sculptor Michael Talbot ARA. He taught at Stafford College, where the course became a model for classical training in the UK.

## Professional recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steven_Whyte&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Professional recognition")]

Whyte became the youngest member of the London-based Society of Portrait Sculptors and was later elected vice president, serving alongside Franta Belsky PPRBS. His early public works in the UK include:

*   _Silverdale Mining Memorial_
*   _Lance Sergeant Jack Baskeyfield VC Tribute_
*   _The Spirit of 1948_

## Move to the United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steven_Whyte&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Move to the United States")]

In 2004, Whyte relocated to Carmel, California, where he opened the Steven Whyte Sculpture Studios and Gallery. The studio quickly gained attention and became a cultural landmark. Media features included CNN's _My City My Secret_, _The San Francisco Chronicle_, and _The New York Times_ in its _36 Hours_ travel column. After thirteen years in the U.S., Whyte became a naturalized American citizen.

## Monumental works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steven_Whyte&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Monumental works")]

Whyte is known for large-scale public monuments that blend classical technique with contemporary themes. Major commissions include:

*   **The National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military** (San Diego, CA) – Featuring Bob Hope surrounded by historically accurate service members from each major conflict in which he performed.
*   **Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Monuments**
    *   _Column of Knowledge_ (Fontana, CA) – A bust of King atop a column representing books that influenced him.
    *   Monument (Hollywood, FL) – A 1.5x life-size bust atop a granite slab engraved with the "I Have a Dream" speech.

*   **High Relief at Mission San Carlos Borromeo** (Carmel, CA) – Depicting St. Anthony and the Christ Child.
*   **U.S. Presidents Series** – Busts of Abraham Lincoln, Thomas Jefferson, and others. A Lincoln bust was displayed by former secretary of defense Leon Panetta at the Pentagon.
*   **Texas A&M University**
    *   _John David Crow Monument_ – A 13-foot statue of the Heisman Trophy winner.
    *   _War Hymn Monument_ – A 1.6x life-size group of twelve students in mid-cheer.

*   **San Diego Law Enforcement Memorial** – A sheriff presenting a folded flag to a fallen comrade’s family.
*   **Tufts University** – A life-size bronze elephant, _Jumbo_, the school’s mascot.
*   **Cannery Row Monument** (Monterey, CA) – Features John Steinbeck and characters from his novel _Cannery Row_; the largest public monument between San Francisco and Los Angeles.
*   **Comfort Women Memorials** – Located in San Francisco and Seoul, these commemorate the estimated 200,000 women forced into sexual slavery by the Japanese military in WWII. The San Francisco monument was named one of _Smithsonian Magazine’s_ top monuments of 2017.
*   **Joseph Vaughn Monument** (Furman University, SC) – Celebrating the university’s first Black student.
*   **Florida Slavery Memorial** – Currently in progress.
*   **Fred Gray Tribute** (Alabama) – Honoring the civil rights attorney who represented Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King Jr.
*   **Crossroads Veterans Monument** (Dublin, CA) – A $500,000 installation honoring U.S. veterans.
*   Local tributes – Including portraits of Mike Marotta (Monterey, CA) and Dennis Capra (Swiss Rifle Club).

## Style and philosophy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steven_Whyte&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Style and philosophy")]

Whyte’s work emphasizes expressive presence, detailed realism, and classical craftsmanship. He is known for blending technical rigor with emotional depth. His sculptures range from intimate portrait busts to large public monuments and frequently explore themes of identity, resilience, and representation.

## Awards and recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steven_Whyte&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Awards and recognition")]

*   2016 – Sports Artist of the Year, United States Sports Academy
*   Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery – Bronze bust of Congressman John Conyers, Jr. added to the permanent collection
*   The Carter Center – Heroic bust of President Jimmy Carter (3.3x life-size)
*   2021 – Stanley Bleifeld Memorial Award, National Sculpture Society
*   2022 – Champion of the Arts, Monterey County
*   2022 – Recognized by the U.S. Congress and California Senate for contributions to the arts
*   2024 – Elected Fellow of the National Sculpture Society

## Artistic style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steven_Whyte&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Artistic style")]

The human form is Whyte's preferred subject, and he typically works with live models whenever possible. His sculptures are ultimately cast in bronze, but they begin as clay.

Steven Whyte describes himself as a "sculptor of people"[[2]](

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Type of surrender

For other uses, see [Unconditional surrender (disambiguation)](link_1).

An **unconditional surrender** is a [surrender](link_2) in which no guarantees, reassurances, or promises (i.e., conditions) are given to the surrendering party. It is often demanded with the threat of complete destruction, extermination or annihilation.

Announcing that only unconditional surrender is acceptable puts psychological pressure on a weaker adversary, but it may also prolong hostilities. A party typically only demands unconditional surrender when it has a significant advantage over their adversaries, when victory is thought to be inevitable.

In modern times, unconditional surrenders most often include guarantees provided by [international law](link_3). In some cases, surrender is truly accepted unconditionally; while in other cases terms are offered and accepted, but forces are declared to be subject to "unconditional surrender" for symbolic purposes. This type of surrender may also be accepted by the surrendering party under the expectation of guarantees agreed to informally.

## Examples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unconditional_surrender&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Examples")]

### Banu Qurayza during Muhammad's era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unconditional_surrender&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Banu Qurayza during Muhammad's era")]

Main article: [Banu Qurayza](link_4)

After the [Battle of the Trench](link_5), in which the Muslims tactically overcame their opponents while suffering very few casualties, efforts to defeat the Muslims failed, and [Islam](link_6) became influential in the region. As a consequence, the Muslim army besieged the neighbourhood of the [Jewish](link_7)[Banu Qurayza tribe](link_8), leading to their unconditional surrender. All the men, apart from a few who converted to [Islam](link_6), were executed, while the women and children were [enslaved](link_9).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender#cite_note-Peterson-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender#cite_note-Ramadan140-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender#cite_note-Brown,_p._81-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender#cite_note-Lings229-5) The historicity of the incident has been questioned.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender#cite_note-6)

### Napoleon Bonaparte

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unconditional_surrender&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Napoleon Bonaparte")]

When [Napoleon Bonaparte](link_10) escaped from his enforced exile on the island of [Elba](link_11), one of the steps that the delegates of the European powers at the [Congress of Vienna](link_12) took was to issue a statement on 13 March 1815 [declaring Napoleon Bonaparte](link_13) to be an outlaw. The text includes the following paragraphs:

> By thus breaking [the convention](link_14) which had established him in the island of Elba, Bonaparte destroys the only legal title on which his existence depended, and by appearing again in France, with projects of confusion and disorder, he has deprived himself of the protection of the law, and has manifested to the universe that there can be neither peace nor truce with him.
> 
> 
> The powers consequently declare, that Napoleon Bonaparte has placed himself without the pale of civil and social relations; and that, as an enemy and disturber of the tranquillity of the world, he has rendered himself liable to public vengeance.

—Plenipotentiaries of the high powers who signed the [Treaty of Paris (1814)](link_15).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender#cite_note-7)

Consequently, as Napoleon was considered an [outlaw](link_16) when he surrendered to Captain [Frederick Maitland](link_17) of [HMS _Bellerophon_](link_18) at the end of the [Hundred Days](link_19), he was not protected by military law or international law as a head of state and so the British were under no legal obligation to either accept his surrender or to spare his life.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender#cite_note-8) However, they did so to prevent him from being a [martyr](link_20) and exiled him to the remote [South Atlantic](link_21) island of [Saint Helena](link_22).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### American Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unconditional_surrender&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: American Civil War")]

The most famous early use of the phrase in the [American Civil War](link_23) occurred during the 1862 [Battle of Fort Donelson](link_24). [Brigadier General](link_25)[Ulysses S. Grant](link_26) of the [Union Army](link_27) received a request for terms from [Confederate](link_28) Brigadier General [Simon Bolivar Buckner Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Bolivar_Buckner_Sr [link_29]. "Simon Bolivar Buckner Sr."), the fort's commanding officer. Grant's reply was that "no terms except an unconditional and immediate surrender can be accepted. # USS Midway Aircraft Carrier Museum in San Diego

Recently Amie and I spent the weekend in San Diego and tried to do a lot of the attractions that we had never done before. From visiting Cabrillo National Monument, to [hiking Cowles Mountain](link_43), to seeing the statues of the greatest generation in the port of San Diego. The last attraction that we had on the list, however, was to visit the USS Midway at the Broadway Pier in Downtown San Diego. I had members of my family serve in the military, one even in the Navy, so being able to tour this ship was a great experience and one I would suggest to anyone.

![Image 4: USS Midway Far Shot](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-Far-Shot-1024x682.jpg)

### History & Information

_“USS Midway was an aircraft carrier of the United States Navy, the lead ship of her class, and the first to be commissioned after the end of World War II. Active in the Vietnam War and in Operation Desert Storm, she is currently a museum ship at the San Diego Aircraft Carrier Museum in San Diego, California. She is the only remaining US aircraft carrier of the World War II era that is not an Essex-class ship. When she was completed in 1945, she was the first US warship that was unable to utilize the Panama Canal due to her size. On 10 January 2004, the ship was moored at her final location at the Broadway Pier in downtown San Diego, where she was opened to the public on 7 June 2004. In the first year of operation, the museum doubled attendance projections by welcoming 879,281 guests aboard.”_

The ship is open most days from 10 AM to 5 PM and costs $18 for adults (as of 2014). Once you board the ship, the tour is what you make of it. There is an audio tour that you can take with your headset, or you can simply wander the hallways of this famous ship and marvel at what life must have been like for the sailors. There are also 25 different types of helicopters and planes on top of the ship and flight simulators and other activities for the kids. We opted for the self guided tour and began our exploration.

### The Interior Decks

What I immediately noticed when walking down to the interior of the boat was that it was not made for people like me. I am 6’3″ and had to duck while walking through doors. If you are much taller than me, you may not like browsing the interior of the ship as it seems to get smaller and smaller; however, it is worth the lack of comfort to see all of the unique sites.

![Image 6: USS Midway small quarters](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-small-quarters-682x1024.jpg)

I am too tall

We spent some time walking around the kitchen, which had about 20 tables and a small line where the food could be served before walking further into the ship to the sickbay and dentist area. The sickbay is not somewhere you would want to be while on the ship. It looked like it would make me sicker to be down here with the intensely close quarters and realistic drilling sound they have in the dentist offices. I was not a fan, but it was interesting to see.

![Image 7: USS Midway sickbay beds](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-sickbay-beds-1024x682.jpg)

This alone makes me sick

![Image 8: USS Midway communicators](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-communicators-1024x682.jpg)

From there, we headed into the engine room and saw the colossal engine that propelled a boat of this size. One of the people there informed us that this was one of four engine rooms, which is crazy to think about. All of the grating you walk on is see-through, and you can see parts of the engine below it, almost like a scene out of Aliens.

![Image 9: USS Midway walkway](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-walkway-1024x682.jpg)

![Image 10: USS Midway stairs to the hull](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-stairs-to-the-hull-682x1024.jpg)

From there, we headed to the jail. The jail was a collection of tiny compartments to hold the higher offenders as well as one large room for the people who needed a night to readjust themselves. If you are claustrophobic, this is not where you would want to end up. You can even pose for pictures next to the fake jail cells if you so desire. They also have lots of wax figures everywhere which make for some funny photos.

![Image 11: USS Midway jail](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-jail-682x1024.jpg)

![Image 12: USS Midway wax figures](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-wax-figures-1024x682.jpg)

### Flight Deck & Planes

After spending an hour in the Interior decks, we headed up to the Flight Deck to check out the planes and the admiral and captain’s quarters. The aircraft alone were worth the price of admission for me as they were from many different eras and were exciting to check out. You can even sit inside a plane for pictures and walk inside many different types of helicopters. What is immediately evident is how little amount of space they have to take off, and it gave me a much better understanding of how difficult this must be. Check out some of the pictures below.

![Image 13: Helicoper Plane](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Helicoper-Plane-1024x682.jpg)

![Image 14: Sitting in plane USS Midway](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Sitting-in-plane-USS-Midway-1024x682.jpg)

![Image 15: Plane Upclose](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Plane-Upclose-1024x682.jpg)

Next, we headed into the Admiral and Captain Quarters, and I have to say this is the place to be on the boat. They have their private kitchen where cooks can cook for them, as well as living rooms, full bathrooms, and even couches. They also had an entire war room complete with maps and chairs situated around a table, just like in all of the great war movies.

![Image 16: Control tower](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Control-tower--1024x682.jpg)

Why is there an American Idol flag…

![Image 17: USS Midway flight deck with San Deigo behind](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/USS-Midway-flight-deck-with-San-Deigo-behind-682x1024.jpg)

After this, we headed back down to the Hanger Deck to look through the shops before leaving. You could easily spend a whole day here as we walked around for at least 2 hours and didn’t see it all before we headed out. It is a remarkable experience if you are into machinery and military history,and even if you are not, I would still recommend it. Make sure to leave me a comment if you enjoyed it as well.

# Best WordPress Map Plugins (2026)

_Last updated: October 3, 2026. Disclosure: this page is published by the developer of MapPress, which is on the list. Install counts and ratings are from WordPress.org; prices are from each vendor’s site._

## The short answer

*   **Best free map plugin overall:** MapPress. Unlimited maps and markers, clustering and rich popups for free, no API key, and maps are edited right in the WordPress editor.
*   **Biggest user base:** WP Go Maps, with 300,000+ installs, though its free version allows only one map.
*   **Best dedicated store locator:** WP Store Locator, free, with search by address and opening hours.
*   **Best for region maps** (colored countries or states): MapGeo.
*   **Best for developers who like shortcodes:** Leaflet Map, free and open source.

## Comparison at a glance

| Plugin | Best for | Free version | Paid from | Active installs | Rating |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **MapPress** | Most sites: free, unlimited, no API key | Unlimited maps, clustering, popups, directions | $39/year (3 sites) | 30,000+ | 4.7 (147) |
| **WP Go Maps** | Bulk import/export, visitor-submitted markers | One map only | $69 one-time (1 site) | 300,000+ | 4.8 (3,000+) |
| **WP Maps** | Location listings with search in the free version | Unlimited maps, listings, filters | $39/year (3 sites) or $59 lifetime (1 site) | 60,000+ | 4.3 (122) |
| **WP Store Locator** | A dedicated store locator | Full store locator with hours and search | Paid add-ons (CSV import, statistics) | 40,000+ | 4.8 (312) |
| **Leaflet Map** | Developers comfortable with shortcodes | Everything; no paid version | Free | 30,000+ | 4.9 (58) |
| **MapGeo** | Colored region maps (countries, states) | Unlimited vector maps | $39.99/year (1 site) | 40,000+ | 4.5 (64) |
| **Maps Marker Pro** | Layered maps and GPX tracks | Free version retired in 2020 | €49 (1 site, 1 year of updates) | Paid only | — |

## The plugins

### 1. MapPress

The best all-round free map plugin. The free version has unlimited maps and markers, popups with images and links, animated marker clustering, directions and KML/GPX tracks. Maps default to free OpenStreetMap tiles from OpenFreeMap with no API key and no cookies, and you can switch to Google Maps or Mapbox anytime. You build maps right in the Gutenberg or classic editor.

Pro ($39/year for 3 sites) adds searchable, filterable maps with visitor location and nearest-first results, custom icons, popup and list templates, and maps generated from custom fields and ACF.

**Limits:** no export of locations, and a smaller user base than WP Go Maps.

### 2. WP Go Maps

A long feature list, most across paid add-ons. Pro is a one-time license from $69, and clustering is in a separate Gold add-on.

**Limits:** the free version allows just one map; popups with images and directions need Pro; marker clustering costs extra even on top of Pro; and maps are built on a separate admin screen rather than in the editor. Its changelog also lists a string of security fixes in 2025–26, including cross-site scripting and unauthenticated database access.

### 3. WP Maps

Strong free features for location lists: unlimited maps, searchable and filterable listings below the map, clustering and Google, OpenStreetMap or Mapbox tiles. Pro is $39/year (3 sites, bundled with the vendor’s other plugins) or $59 lifetime for one site.

**Limits:** the lowest rating here (4.3), with about 1 in 8 reviews at one star, citing bugs and unanswered support requests. Pro is sold mainly as a membership bundled with 40+ of the vendor’s other plugins, and radius search and post integration need it.

### 4. WP Store Locator

A dedicated store locator rather than a general map plugin: search by address or postcode, visitor location, opening hours with “open now” badges, and a landing page per location. Works with OpenStreetMap for free, or Google, Mapbox and Stadia with a key.

**Limits:** it only does store locators, so it’s no help for event maps, travel routes or maps in posts. CSV import is a paid add-on, and the vendor has announced a Pro version, which may move features out of the free plugin.

### 5. Leaflet Map

Free and open source, with markers, shapes, GeoJSON, KML and GPX through shortcodes. No API key needed.

**Limits:** no visual map editor: every map, marker and shape is typed as a shortcode, so it suits developers more than content editors.

### 6. MapGeo (Interactive Geo Maps)

For a different job: colored vector maps of countries, states or regions, with tooltips and click actions. 250+ base maps.

**Limits:** not a street map. Clustering, custom markers and legends need Pro ($39.99/year per site), and recent reviews mention slow support and licensing problems.

### 7. Maps Marker Pro

A paid-only plugin for layered maps, GPX tracks and marker management, with a 30-day trial. Licenses from €49 for one site including a year of updates.

**Limits:** no free version (the old free Leaflet Maps Marker plugin was retired in 2020), and updates stop unless you renew, from €35 a year.

## How to choose

*   **You want a few good maps on pages or posts, free, without an API key** → MapPress.
*   **You want maps built from your posts, custom fields or ACF** → MapPress Pro.
*   **You need to export locations or collect markers from visitors** → WP Go Maps Pro.
*   **You run a chain of stores and want hours, “open now” and per-location pages** → WP Store Locator.
*   **You want to color in countries or states** → MapGeo.
*   **You’re a developer happy with shortcodes and want fully free and open source** → Leaflet Map.

See also: [MapPress vs WP Go Maps, free and Pro compared](https://mappresspro.com/mappress-vs-wp-go-maps/).

## FAQ

**What is the best free WordPress map plugin?** For most sites, MapPress: unlimited maps and markers, clustering and popups with images are free, with no API key. If you need a full store locator with opening hours, WP Store Locator is the best free option.

**Which WordPress map plugins work without a Google Maps API key?** MapPress, WP Maps, WP Store Locator and Leaflet Map all offer free OpenStreetMap-based maps with no key. WP Go Maps does too if you choose a keyless engine in setup.

**Which free map plugin allows unlimited maps?** MapPress, WP Maps, Leaflet Map and MapGeo. WP Go Maps’ free version is limited to one map.

**Do I need a Google Maps API key at all?** Only if you want Google’s map tiles. Google requires a key with billing enabled, though most small sites stay within the free usage allowance.

## Sources

# Relief Sculpture

Relief sculpture is a hybrid art form, with one foot in the world of the draftsman and painter, and the other firmly planted in the world of the sculptor. Its greatest asset is the ability to convey a narrative. The portrait in relief has the advantage of portraying a subject from one point of view. This is especially helpful because it allows me to work from photographic reference, which is critical in the case of honoring a person from the past.

# Portrait Sculpture

In over 40 years of making sculpture, I have never tired of making portraits. In the short distance between the hairline, the chin, and the face, a split second can express a wide range of psychological information. My job is to find that moment! The face is a never-ending theater that reveals something profound about our humanity.

[![Image 2](https://eugenedaub.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/port_amelia.jpg)](https://eugenedaub.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/port_amelia-781x1024.jpg)

**Eugene Daub** began his career as an art director for an advertising firm. His first job in sculpture was for The Franklin Mint where he developed skills in relief sculpture.

He taught at the Academy of Art University in San Francisco, Ca from 1993 to 2002. He has been an instructor at the Scottsdale Artists’ School from 1991 to present and is the designer of the first Philadelphia Liberty Medal,which that city awards every year to a champion of world peace.

Daub has exhibited extensively and has worked in numerous public collections, including the Helsinki Art Museum, the British Museum; the Smithsonian Institution; The National Statuary Hall Collection in the United States Capitol and the United States National Park Service.

Daub has created over 40 major monuments in the U.S. in the last 30 years.He is also one of the pioneer members of the American Medallic Sculpture Association, which pushed American contemporary medallic art into the international contemporary movement.

He won both of the nation's highest awards for excellence in medallic art: The Saltus Award from the American Numismatic Society, and the Gold medal, from the American Numismatic Association.

Daub is a Fellow of the National Sculpture Society.

# Rosa Parks

**The Spark that Ignited the Modern Civil Rights Movement**  
**Location:**National Statuary Hall, U.S. Capitol  
**Size/Medium:**8 ft 10.75 in: bronze & granite

Daub & Firmin Studio’s  
Principal sculptor: Eugene Daub  
Design and Concept: Eugene Daub and Rob Firmin

Rosa Parks is deservedly one of the icons of the American civil rights movement. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. said of her act of defiance in Montgomery Alabama on Dec 1, 1955: “The spark that ignited the modern civil rights movement.”

It seems almost everyone knows that Rosa Parks refused to relinquish her bus seat for a white person, but it was a more complex story. Her action vitalized the movement because her impeccable character and supreme dignity made her the right person at the right time. She was not put up to the action by anyone. She did not do it because she was tired. We wanted to capture her character and the character of the historic moment. The background evokes centuries of resistance and the solid support of millions.

We are delighted to have been selected; it is a crowning piece of our civil rights artwork. We thank the NEA, the Architect of the Capitol, its Curator, and the Congressional Committee on the Library for their support.

![Image 1](https://eugenedaub.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/DF-Med-2-American-Numismatic-Society.jpg)

# Art Medal

For centuries the Medal has been a traditional way to pay homage to great people and their efforts.   
They are actually small monuments that show a visage and textual information.   
Most medals have two sides which inherently compliments and marries the obverse and reverse together. For spatial considerations, most medals shown here are only the Front side, or (Obverse). There is also another category of medallic art (scroll down) that are not so traditional. They are pure works of art that seek only to be themselves, unique works of art. As such, they have no boundaries in shape or size or subject. Eugene is one of the pioneer members of AMSA, the American Medallic Sculpture Association. # San Diego Guide: Food, Hiking, Museums & Activities

![Image 3](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/san-diego-header.jpg)

San Diego is one of the reasons that people visit / move to California. This city by the beach is full of amazing vistas and eye catching attractions at every turn. Exploring its many hidden wonders has been a call for adventurers for decades yet there is always something new being found. While I haven’t explored as much as others, I have spent some time in this fascinating city. The guide below will help to facilitate a week of exploration in one of California’s most beautiful places.**Click on the image to learn more about each spot**and be sure to check back as more places will get added as I explore them.

What is a better place to start in the exploration of a city than its culinary options? Again, this list is by no means exclusive, it is just the places I have visited thus far. Whether its donuts and pizza or tacos and BBQ, San Diego has something for everyone.

## San Diego History

Many people consider San Diego as the original California. In 1542, Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo, a Spanish explorer, discovered San Diego Bay. He was searching for a fabled cross-continent water route known as the Strait of Anian. Cabrillo was the first explorer to map a large percentage of California’s coastal features. In 1602, Sebastian Vizcaíno named the area for a saint, San Diego de Alcalá. He mapped the California coast in greater detail.

**Establishment of the San Diego Mission**

By 1767, Gaspar de Portola is appointed to the governorship by Spain. Five groups were sent to settle the area. Sea passage is difficult in 1769, and 21 sailors died, others suffered with scurvy. The San Diego Mission was then established on Presidio Hill and was the first of 21 missions to be built. More than 1,400 indigenous people lived near the mission.

The first American colonists arrived in 1774. Two years later, in 1776, a new fortress was built at the Presidio. The Presidio’s total settlement population was about two hundred people in 1790. Twenty years later, Fort Guijarros was constructed.

**San Diego’s Earthquakes**

A large earthquake hit San Diego in November 1800. Geoscientists believe the quake registered at approximately 6.5 Richter scale. The earthquake damaged San Diego and San Juan Capistrano missions. In 1812, an earthquake destroyed the San Diego mission again.

**San Diego’s Early 19th Century Homes**

In the 1820s decade, San Diego’s population grew to six hundred people. Home building throughout today’s Old Town began in earnest. Adobes of Pio Pico (the Governor of California in 1845) and Maria Reyes Ibanez were constructed at the intersection of Wallace and Juan Streets.

The homes of Rosario Aguilar, Jose Antonio Estudillo, Dona Tomasa Alvarado, and Juan Bandini followed. The home are built in traditional Spanish-Mexican style. San Diego was ruled by Mexico for approximately 25 years.

**San Diego’s Land Grants, the Ranchos**

Mexico granted the first rancho, Los Peñasquitos, of 8,486 acres to Captain Francisco María Ruíz. Thereafter, 33 additional land grants representing a total area of 948 square miles were awarded in the area. San Diego was then the “unofficial” capital of California because of Governor Jose Maria Echandia’s preference.

In 1828, a massive smallpox outbreak occurred. Vaccinations, a relatively new procedure, helped to stall the epidemic. In 1832, smallpox killed many natives and some of the missions were closed during this time

Richard Henry Dana’s account, “Two Years Before the Mast,” (1841) recounts adventures and dangers of traveling to San Diego. Rattlesnakes and bears were apparently plentiful. San Diego, he said, was not an easy place to live.

If you are spending any amount of time in some of California’s best cities then let these guides be an inspiration for where to start your exploration. Some of the cities have more recommendations than others, but all of them are full of unique adventures and will continue to grow as I explore more. Please leave your recommendations in the comments of each city if you have a spot you think I should check out and have fun exploring. **Click the image below to explore my recommendations in each city.**

## Big Bear

[![Image 5](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/Castle-Rock-19.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/big-bear-city-guide)

Big Bear is a popular Southern California mountain town close to Los Angeles and the Inland Empire. Here are all of my favorite things to do there.

## Los Angeles

[![Image 6](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/LA-Observation-Deck-5.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/los-angeles-guide)

Explore the City of Angels and the birthplace of the movies with this guide that features everything from Hollywood Sign hikes to the best donuts.

## Malibu

[![Image 7](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/Point-Dume-Malibu.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/malibu-guide)

Malibu is not just a playground for the rich and famous, it is also a great place for beaches, hiking, and seafood. Check out all of my favorite spots.

## Mendocino

[![Image 8](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/mendocino-headlands-3.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/mendocino-guide)

Mendocino is one of the most popular getaways for Bay Area residents and it is easy to see why when you visit. This small coastal town has tons of restaurants, hikes, and activities all located right on the ocean. Read one for some of my favorite spots in the area.

## Napa

[![Image 9](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/napa-featured-1.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/napa-city-guide)

Napa is world renowned for its wine, but the city of Napa also has a lot of great restaurants, wine tasting rooms, and outdoor activities.

## Oakland

[![Image 10](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/oakland-24-hours-1.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/oakland-city-guide)

Across the bay from San Francisco, Oakland is home to many up and coming areas and restaurants. It is a great place to spend a weekend exploring.

## Palm Springs

[![Image 11](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/Hard-Rock-Hotel-10.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/palm-springs-guide)

Visit this famous desert getaway spot with a guide that showcases its rich food scene, museums, and outdoor activities. Even in the heat of summer, there is something for everyone here.

## San Diego

[![Image 12](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/sunset-cliffs-22.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/san-diego-guide)

This relaxing city, right on the water is the perfect place for a weekend of exploration among the fantastic beaches, beautiful hiking trails and even better eateries.

## Sacramento

[![Image 13](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Tower-Bridge-1.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/sacramento-guide)

The state’s capitol is home to lots of unique museums and history as well as a farm to fork revival in the many different restaurants across the city.

## San Francisco

[![Image 14](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/golden-gate-bridge-1.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/san-francisco-guide)

The home of the Golden Gate bridge is a city full of adventure and charm. Wander the Palace of Fine Arts or indulge in fantastic seafood while in a city you will never want to leave.

## Santa Barbara

[![Image 15](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/santa-barbara-view-1.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/santa-barbara-guide)

Santa Barbara is one of the most famous coastal cities in Southern California and its home to many unique restaurants and outdoor activities. Whether it’s eating great ice cream or walking along the water, Santa Barbara has something for everyone.

## Sonoma

[![Image 16](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/sonoma-main-1.jpg)](https://californiathroughmylens.com/sonoma-guide)

As one of California’s most famous wine regions, Sonoma is an amazing place to explore. Check out my favorite restaurants, wineries, and adventures in this guide.

If your favorite city isn’t on the list yet, check out my[map of locations](https://californiathroughmylens.com/map-of-locations/)for all of the spots I have written about in California.

# Los Angeles Guide: Food, Hikes, Free Attractions, Museums & Shopping

![Image 3](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/los-angeles-top.jpg)

Los Angeles is just one of those cities that you have to spend time at one point in your life. People come from all around the world to walk among the stars, marvel at the Hollywood Sign and relax on its beaches. I have been dozens of times and am still pulling back the different layers of the onion that make up one of the United States most famous cities. I have never been one to just do the normal tourist attractions though, so this guide is full of ideas ranging from donuts to hikes that will let you explore the unique side of this famous city.**Click the photo to read a post**on that specific item and to start your journey exploring this famous city. Be sure to let me know your favorite spots in the comments.

# Donuts

What’s not to love about these delicious circles of sugar and carbs? Honestly, I could eat donuts every day if I thought it was good for me. The LA donut game is strong as well, here are my favorites in the city.

# San Francisco Guide: Food, Hiking, Hotels & Free Activities

![Image 3](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/san-fran-header.jpg)

You will never forget the first time you see the Golden Gate Bridge, the way the modern marvel rises across the ocean is a sight to behold. That is just the beginning of the fantastic adventure that San Francisco has in store for you though. Whether it’s exploring the Palace of Fine Arts, eating at the exclusive Swan Oyster Depot or just walking Pier 39 there is a wealth of experiences to be had in this famous California city. You can see some of my favorite spots below and be sure to click on the image to learn more about each one. Let me know what your favorite place is in the comments so I can keep adding new adventures to this guide.

# San Francisco Free Attractions

San Francisco, like any big city, can be an expensive place to visit. There are a bunch of great activities that you can see without spending any money though such as walking the mosaic steps, exploring the wave organ and visiting the Palace of Fine Arts. You can see my favorite free activities below.

## San Francisco History

Before permanent European settlers arrived in the San Francisco Bay area, the first European explorers sailed California coastline in the 1500s. Indigenous peoples, including the Yelamu tribal band, lived here.

In 1769, the Portola expedition arrived and noted the typical fog. The Mission was established in 1776. By 1786, Juan Bautiza de Anza and his settlement party from San Diego came to establish a mission and presidio. The Mission of St. Francis of Assisi (Mission San Francisco de Asis) became the center of material and spiritual life for more than a thousand Native Americans in the area.

**Early Spanish-Mexican Rulers and American Control**

Mexico declared independence from Spain and became a nation in 1821. Historians say this period initiated the decline of the missions in California. By 1835, William Richardson, an American, permanently settled in Yerba Buena.

Five years later, more Americans came west to “Alta California.” The Americans wanted an independent California and, for a short while, the California Republic existed. James B. Montgomery arrived in July 1846 to fly the United States flag in the plaza, now Portsmouth Square.

For a short while, San Francisco became known as Yerba Buena. In 1847, the city returned to its former name when Alta California leader, Don Vallejo, agreed that the “new” city bear the name of his dear wife, Doña Francisca Benicia Carrillo.

**San Francisco and the Gold Rush**

Gold was first found in the California foothills near Sacramento in 1848. San Francisco was the central entry point and depot of explorers in search of gold.

Although no U.S. census record exists for the area in 1850, historians say the population grew from about 1,000 to at least 25,000 people.

As more frenzied explorers decided to call the area home, the 1860 census figures show that almost 57,000 people lived here. Some of the wooden ships arriving during the Gold Rush were later dismantled to build the now expanding harbor.

The three years of 1849, 1850, and 1851 were wild, reckless, and lawless. Prostitutes and gamblers were plentiful because some miners did strike it rich. Six large fires also broke out at this time.

**Nevada’s Silver Boom, Railroads, Golden Gate Park, and Cable Cars**

In 1859, a major silver find was announced in Nevada at Comstock Lode. Residents now made money as people stocked mining supplies to once more head for the hills.

The Central Pacific Railroad’s construction began, and several of the city’s captains of industry imported thousands of Chinese people to build the tracks. Chinatown in San Francisco rapidly grew to the largest Chinese population and settlement in the Western world.

By 1887, San Francisco urban planners designated a thousand acres on the Pacific peninsula to build Golden Gate Park. Cable cars now spanned the city to enable residents to traverse steep hills.

# Palm Springs Guide: Celebrity Homes, Museums, Shopping, Food & Hikes

![Image 3](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/palm-springs-main.jpg)

For decades Palm Springs has been a playground for both the rich and famous and the weekend warriors. During the summer it reaches over 110 degrees, but that doesn’t stop people from flocking to its pools and activities. I prefer visiting in the winter as it is less busy and it allows me to spend more time hiking and exploring some of the rich outdoor opportunities available at only a stones through from the city. Browse some of my favorite museums, restaurants and outdoor activities below and let me know what your favorite spot is in the comments so I can keep adding new adventures to this guide.

# Palm Springs Restaurants

Palm Springs is full to the brim with amazing culinary spots. One of the top rated pizza places in the US is here (Bill’s) and Cheeky’s is one of my personal favorite spots in the area. Even the restaurant in the Hard Rock Hotel is fantastic and keeps me coming back for more, here are a few of my favorites.

# Historical Structures

People have been living in California for centuries, and during that time, many historical structures have been created. Take a trip back in time and check out some of California’s lost history. Head to a Nike Missile Site to see a piece of the mid-20th century, or if you’re looking to go even farther back, head near Joshua Tree National Park and scope out some of the mines that gave the state its nickname. Alternatively, if you want to see some of California’s oldest artifacts, head over to the Blythe Intaligos. There are lots of historical structures in California that are worth the visit.

# Charles Bukowski: San Pedro plans to honor star writer after tourist demand

This article is more than 7 years old

A historian is raising funds to immortalize the cult writer and poet ahead of his centennial birthday next year

[Andrew Gumbel](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/andrew-gumbel)

Tue 20 Aug 2019 01.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 20 Aug 2019 10.06 EDT

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

A s the unofficial historian of San Pedro, the rough but charming working-class port of the city of [Los Angeles](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/los-angeles), Angela Romero fields one question more than any other: where is the monument to Charles Bukowski?

German tour companies want to know. So do large numbers of casual visitors who routinely make the 25-mile trek from downtown LA to learn more about the cult writer, boozehound, and confessional poet of the damned who made San Pedro his final home.

And the answer, up to now, has always been the same: sorry, we don’t have one.

Lack of affection for Bukowski is not the problem, even if the mainstream literary world tends to look down on him as a [cheap-trick populist](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2005/03/14/smashed), and his frank writing about bedding women – and standing in awe of “[so much breast and ass](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/49569/a-340-dollar-horse-and-a-hundred-dollar-whore)” – doesn’t exactly jibe with our #MeToo cultural moment.

![Image 3: A stencil of poet Charles Bukowski, by Elvis Segarich, adorns a window in San Pedro.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f0de152d26c54867f9775517a723ac42af0f5661/0_55_3024_3780/master/3024.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)[View image in fullscreen](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/aug/19/charles-bukowski-san-pedro-plans-to-honor-star-writer-after-tourist-demand?CMP=share_btn_link#img-2)

A stencil of poet Charles Bukowski, by Elvis Segarich, adorns a window in San Pedro. Photograph: Andrew Gumbel/The Guardian

Rather, San Pedro has been slow to realize just how passionate an international following Bukowski still commands a quarter-century after his death at the age of 73. But Romero – curator of a virtual museum of San Pedro history – is determined to change that.

“Fans of Bukowski travel to San Pedro from all around the world looking for a way to feel close to a man whose words touched them so deeply,” she says. “They’re looking to experience even a small part of the town he chose as his final home.”

With support from San Pedro’s business leaders, arts community and city council district office, Romero has found a local [sculptor](https://eugenedaub.com/) with a long track record of producing public art to immortalize Bukowski in bronze. And she has launched a [GoFundMe](https://www.gofundme.com/bukowski) campaign to raise the $150,000 she estimates it will take to do him justice.

The campaign kicked off last weekend with a crowded 99th birthday party for Bukowski held at one of his favorite local coffee shops, Sacred Grounds, complete with poetry readings, testimonials from those who knew him, a cake, and an unexpected last-minute appearance by his widow, Linda Lee Bukowski, who declared herself “over the moon”.

A majority of the participants were women, none of whom expressed slightest misgiving about Bukowski’s outpouring of poems and autobiographical novels in which he portrayed himself as an existential hero making an idiosyncratic pilgrim’s progress through a world of flophouses, dive bars, cheap women and casual vulgarity. He claimed never to have written sober, saying the best writing came out of him like “hot turds” after a night of drinking.

> What people appreciate most is the realness in his writing ... He was very honest about who he was and how he felt

Angela Romero
“He definitely wouldn’t survive if he was starting out now,” Romero acknowledged. “But what people appreciate most is the realness in his writing … He was very honest about who he was and how he felt.”

Branimir Kvartuc, who works for the local city councilman, was similarly dismissive of subjecting Bukowski to any sort of #MeToo acid test. “He didn’t have any status over anybody,” Kvartuc said. “That’s the difference.”

Certainly, the love for his writing was palpable in the room. Andrea Kowalski, who owned the now-defunct Vinegar Hill independent bookstore, recalled throwing a birthday party for Bukowski while he was still alive – his last, as it turned out – and being endlessly touched when he showed up. She read a letter of Bukowski’s in which he wrote: “Women are strange. They are positive; they want to build swimming pools when you are still wondering … how the hell the water bill is going to be paid.”

Bukowski lived in penury most of his life and found redemption through writing, much like other Los Angeles authors dwelling among the defeated and the downtrodden: Nathanael West (who wrote Day of the Locust), John Fante (Ask The Dust) and John Rechy (City of Night). By the time Mickey Rourke played Bukowski in Barfly, a fictionalized movie version of his life that came out in 1987, he was already enjoying a late flowering of commercial success on a scale that most poets only dream about.

He moved to San Pedro in 1978, after marrying Linda, and settled into a relatively quiet existence of writing, hanging out in bars and coffee shops, and sneaking into bookstores where he made a habit of secretly signing copies of his books. Sometimes, admirers would see him walking with wine bottles clutched between his knuckles.

**John Daniel Baskeyfield**[VC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Cross "Victoria Cross") (18 November 1922– 20 September 1944) was a [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army") soldier and an English recipient of the [Victoria Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Cross "Victoria Cross") (VC), the highest award for gallantry in the face of the enemy that can be awarded to members of the British and [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") armed forces.

Born in 1922, Baskeyfield was [called up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_the_United_Kingdom "Conscription in the United Kingdom") to the British Army in early 1942. He served with the 2nd Battalion, [South Staffordshire Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Staffordshire_Regiment "South Staffordshire Regiment"), a [glider infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glider_infantry "Glider infantry") unit of the [1st Airlanding Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Airlanding_Brigade_(United_Kingdom) "1st Airlanding Brigade (United Kingdom)"), part of the [1st Airborne Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Airborne_Division_(United_Kingdom) "1st Airborne Division (United Kingdom)"), in [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_invasion_of_Sicily "Allied invasion of Sicily") and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_invasion_of_Italy "Allied invasion of Italy") in 1943 before returning to the United Kingdom. The division was next deployed in [Operation Market Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Market_Garden "Operation Market Garden") and fought in the subsequent [Battle of Arnhem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Arnhem "Battle of Arnhem").

While defending the Oosterbeek perimeter three days into the battle, Baskeyfield commanded a pair of [anti-tank guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-tank_gun "Anti-tank gun") that destroyed several enemy tanks before the crews were killed. Baskeyfield subsequently fired the guns alone before he too was killed. His body was not identified after the war and he has no known grave.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Baskeyfield&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

John Baskeyfield was born on 18 November 1922 in [Burslem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burslem "Burslem"), [Stoke-on-Trent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke-on-Trent "Stoke-on-Trent"), England,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Baskeyfield#cite_note-BBC-1) the son of Daniel and Minnie Baskeyfield.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Baskeyfield#cite_note-CWGC-2) He trained and worked as a butcher during the early years of the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), until he received his call up papers in February 1942 at the age of 19.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Baskeyfield#cite_note-BBC-1)

## Early military service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Baskeyfield&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early military service")]

Baskeyfield joined the [South Staffordshire Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Staffordshire_Regiment "South Staffordshire Regiment") and served with the 2nd Battalion's [anti-tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-tank "Anti-tank")[platoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platoon "Platoon"). The 2nd Battalion was part of the [1st Airlanding Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Airlanding_Brigade_(United_Kingdom) "1st Airlanding Brigade (United Kingdom)"), itself part of the [1st Airborne Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Airborne_Division_(United_Kingdom) "1st Airborne Division (United Kingdom)") and Baskeyfield accompanied them to North Africa, from where they took part in [Operation Ladbroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Ladbroke "Operation Ladbroke"), the glider-borne element of the [Invasion of Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_invasion_of_Sicily "Allied invasion of Sicily") in 1943. The division then landed in Italy as part of [Operation Slapstick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Slapstick "Operation Slapstick") and spent some weeks fighting their way through the country before sailing back to England.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Baskeyfield#cite_note-MoD-3)

## Battle of Arnhem

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Baskeyfield&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Battle of Arnhem")]

The [Battle of Arnhem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Arnhem "Battle of Arnhem") was part of [Operation Market Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Market_Garden "Operation Market Garden"), an attempt to secure a string of bridges through the Netherlands. At [Arnhem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnhem "Arnhem") the [British 1st Airborne Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_1st_Airborne_Division "British 1st Airborne Division") and [Polish 1st Independent Parachute Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_1st_Independent_Parachute_Brigade "Polish 1st Independent Parachute Brigade") were tasked with securing bridges across the [Lower Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Rhine "Lower Rhine"), the final objectives of the operation. However, the airborne forces that dropped on 17 September were not aware that the [9th SS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_SS_Panzer_Division_Hohenstaufen "9th SS Panzer Division Hohenstaufen") and [10th SS Panzer divisions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10th_SS_Panzer_Division_Frundsberg "10th SS Panzer Division Frundsberg") were also near Arnhem for rest and refit.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Baskeyfield#cite_note-4) Their presence added a substantial number of [Panzergrenadiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panzergrenadiers "Panzergrenadiers"), [tanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank "Tank") and [self-propelled guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-propelled_gun "Self-propelled gun") to the German defences and the Allies suffered heavily in the ensuing battle. Only a small force managed to hold one end of the [Arnhem road bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnhem_road_bridge "Arnhem road bridge") before being overrun on 21 September. The rest of the division became trapped in a small pocket west of the bridge and had to be evacuated on 25 September in [Operation Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Berlin_(Arnhem_rescue) "Operation Berlin (Arnhem rescue)"). The Allies failed to cross the Rhine, which remained under German control until Allied offensives in March 1945.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Baskeyfield#cite_note-5)

### South Staffordshire's advance

**Simon Bolivar Buckner** ([/ˈ s aɪ m ə n ˈ b ɒ l ɪ v ər ˈ b ʌ k n ər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_SY-mən_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")[_BOL-i-vər_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")[_BUK-nər_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); April 1, 1823– January 8, 1914) was an American soldier, Confederate military officer, and politician. He fought in the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") in the [Mexican–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War "Mexican–American War"). He later fought in the [Confederate States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_Army "Confederate States Army") during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"). After the war, he served as the 30th [governor of Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Kentucky "Governor of Kentucky").

# Port of San Diego Statues: Unconditional Surrender & Bob Hope

If you are in Downtown San Diego, there are a couple of amazing statues located right next to the [USS Midway](https://californiathroughmylens.com/2011/10/uss-midway-aircraft-carrier-museum-in-san-diego/), which are fun to take pictures of and/or with. The first one is Unconditional Surrender by J. Seward Johnson, and it is a 25-foot tall statue of the famous image of a sailor kissing a nurse from WWII. It is well done and beautiful with the sunset or the USS Midway in the background. It also makes for a fun statue to copy with your significant other. According to the website, it is only on loan until August 2010, but I was there in October of 201, and it was still there,so go check it out if you get a chance.

![Image 4: Unconditional Surrender statue at sunset](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Unconditional-Surrender-statue-at-sunset-682x1024.jpg)

![Image 5: Unconditional Surrender and uss midway](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Unconditional-Surrender-and-uss-midway-1024x682.jpg)

![Image 6: Unconditional Surrender from USS Midway](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Unconditional-Surrender-from-USS-Midway-1024x682.jpg)

The other statue that they had there was a 1.3 million dollar statue of Bob Hope entertaining the troops. The price seems a little excessive to me, but the statue was pretty cool. It had Bob Hope standing in the middle with many different soldiers cheering him on as they watch. What was also interesting was that there was a stereo playing audio from some of his times entertaining the troupes while we were there, which added to the experience.

![Image 7: Bob Hope Memorial during the day](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Bob-Hope-Memorial-during-the-day-1024x682.jpg)

![Image 8: Full shot of Bob hope Statue San Diego](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Full-shot-of-Bob-hope-Statue-San-Diego-1024x682.jpg)

![Image 9: Bob Hope Statue Close up black and white](https://californiathroughmylens.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/Bob-Hope-Statue-Close-up-black-and-white-682x1024.jpg)

On the far side, there are also some wall memorials dedicated to members of the armed forces that lost their lives, and all of this is perfectly situated with the USS Midway right behind it.

# The Bob Hope Memorial in San Diego

If you are visiting San Diego, one of the most uplifting public art installations to see is the **Bob Hope Memorial**. It sits right along the bayfront, next to the USS _Midway_ aircraft carrier museum, where thousands of people stroll each year to soak in history and sweeping harbor views.

Created by artists [**Eugene Daub**](https://eugenedaub.com/) and [**Steven Whyte**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Whyte), the memorial is located at **Harbor Drive and the G Street Mole**, a perfect spot where the sea breeze carries the hum of passing ships and the laughter of visitors.

* * *

## Who Was Bob Hope?

Bob Hope was much more than a film and television star. Known worldwide for his sharp wit, impeccable timing, and decades of comedy, his greatest legacy is his enduring connection with U.S. servicemen and women.

Beginning in 1943, Hope dedicated over fifty years of his life to bringing entertainment and comfort to American troops overseas. Whether in Europe during World War II, on the Korean Peninsula, in the jungles of Vietnam, or in desert encampments during the Persian Gulf War, Bob Hope made the trip. His USO shows, often held during the Christmas season, lifted morale during some of the darkest and loneliest times.

These tours were not cushy Hollywood gigs. They were staged in combat zones, on airstrips, and in hastily assembled tents. Hope’s presence was a reminder to the troops that they were not forgotten, that America cared, and that laughter could still be found even in war.

* * *

![Image 3: Bob Hope Memorial Unconditional Surrender](https://www.sandiegovideoproduction.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/IMG_0523-e1761250807261.jpg)

## The Bob Hope Memorial

Of all the monuments in San Diego, this one is my personal favorite because it speaks not only of military service but also of the healing power of humor. Whenever I am near the Embarcadero, I make it a point to stop by and say “hello” to Bob.

The memorial is officially called the **National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military**. It is both moving and playful, a testament to the bond between one entertainer and millions of grateful service members.

On our most recent visit, I noticed that there is no longer any audio emanating from the statue. In the past, you could hear recordings of Bob Hope’s famous one-liners and routines. Without the soundtrack, the memorial feels quieter, though the silent bronzes still manage to tell their story through expression and gesture.

* * *

## Design and Atmosphere

The installation is beautifully staged. Set among a grove of coral trees atop a landscaped mound with broad curving steps, the memorial consists of sixteen larger-than-life bronze figures arranged in a 48-foot diameter circular plaza.

At the center is Bob Hope himself, captured mid-performance, microphone in hand, cracking a joke that you can almost hear. Surrounding him are fifteen bronze figures, men and women representing all five branches of the U.S. military, leaning forward, laughing, clapping, and listening intently.

The sculptures are remarkable in their authenticity. Each figure wears a uniform accurate to the era of Bob’s career: World War II, the Korean War, Vietnam, the Cold War, and the Persian Gulf. You can walk among them, stand shoulder to shoulder with the bronze soldiers, and feel, in a small way, what it might have been like to be in Hope’s audience far from home.

Day or night, the memorial has its own atmosphere. During the day, the harbor sparkles behind it with the USS _Midway_ looming nearby as a reminder of military might. At night, the lighting brings the bronzes to life, casting long shadows that make the scene feel almost theatrical, as though the show is about to begin again.

* * *

## About the Artists

The central sculpture of Bob Hope was created by **Eugene Daub**, a renowned sculptor known for his historical works, while the military audience was crafted by the **Daub Firman Hendrickson Group** and the **Steven Whyte Studio**. Together, they created not just a monument but an experience, a frozen moment in time where humor and history converge.

* * *

![Image 4: Bob Hope Memorial](https://www.sandiegovideoproduction.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/IMG_0526-e1761250931224.jpg)

* * *

## Why Visit

The Bob Hope Memorial is more than just a photo stop along San Diego’s waterfront. It is a celebration of joy, resilience, and the power of human connection in the most difficult of times. Standing there among the bronzes, with the sea air on your face and the hum of the city behind you, you can almost hear Bob’s voice echoing across decades. Even if the recordings no longer play, his presence lingers.

If you are planning a trip to San Diego, make sure this memorial is on your list. Take a moment to smile with Bob, thank the troops, and reflect on the ways art, laughter, and compassion continue to honor those who serve.

## Nearby Attractions

The memorial is located in one of the most vibrant and visitor-friendly parts of San Diego. Within a short walk, you can also enjoy:

*   [**USS _Midway_ Museum**](https://www.midway.org/): A floating aircraft carrier turned museum where you can explore the flight deck, aircraft, and living quarters of sailors.

*   [**Unconditional Surrender Statue**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconditional_surrender): The towering sculpture of the famous World War II kiss, just steps away from the Bob Hope Memorial.

*   [**San Diego Maritime Museum**](https://sdmaritime.org/): A collection of historic ships, including the Star of India, the world’s oldest active sailing ship.

*   [**Seaport Village**](https://www.seaportvillage.com/): A charming bayside shopping and dining area, perfect for grabbing lunch or enjoying a sunset stroll.

*   [**Embarcadero Marina Park**](https://www.tclf.org/embarcadero-marina-park-north-and-south): A wide-open green space along the bay where you can picnic, relax, or catch views of Coronado Island.

*   **[Coronado Island](https://www.sandiegovideoproduction.com/coronado/):**An island reachable by automobile (over the Coronado Bridge) or ferry from the Port of San Diego where you can visit the newly refurbished Hotel Del Coronado and enjoy a walk on the Silver Strand beach.

With so much history, art, and beauty in one area, you can easily spend an entire afternoon wandering from one landmark to the next.

# The Bob Hope Memorial in San Diego

If you are visiting San Diego, then the Bob Hope Memorial is fun to see. It’s right next to the USS Midway floating aircraft carrier museum.

Artists Eugene Daub and Steven Whyte created the installation located at Harbor Drive and the G Street Mole.

Bob Hope, the actor, entertainer, and comedian, is known worldwide for his enduring career as a film and TV star. For generations of U.S. servicemen, his greatest legacy is as a tireless entertainer of troops overseas. For over fifty years starting in 1943, he dedicated himself to entertaining soldiers, sailors, and airmen of the armed forces. He flew out many times to the many battle fronts and remote outposts where US military served throughout the world. Bob’s overseas USO tours, often during the Christmas season, were deeply appreciated and fondly remembered by thousands of servicemen on protracted tours of duty. And often these tours were under combat conditions, far from their homes and families.

### Bob Hope Memorial

This is my personal favorite memorial here in San Diego that honors those who have served their country. So I always make it a point to go and say “hi” to Bob whenever I am in the neighborhood.

Design notes: Located in a grove of coral trees atop a landscaped mound with broad curving steps, the National Salute to Bob Hope and the Military features a grouping of sixteen larger than life-size bronze figures in a 48-foot diameter circular plaza. The figures represent a typical road show with Bob entertaining troops near the front. The focal point is a bronze of Bob Hope himself by renowned sculptor Eugene Daub. Fifteen additional sculptures form an eternal audience representing men and women of the five branches of the U.S. military services. Attractive landscaping and lighting showcase the National Salute for visitors day and night, by land and water.

The troops are Bob Hope’s favorite audience, and beyond them is “Unconditional Surrender” and the USS Midway Museum

About the Sculptures: The bronze figures are sculpted in military uniforms authentic to the various eras of Bob’s career from World War II through the Korean War, Vietnam War, Cold War, and the first Persian Gulf War. The fifteen military bronze figures were designed and fabricated by the Daub Firman Hendrickson Group and the Steven Whyte Studio.

A bronze statue is proposed to honor author Charles Bukowski who lived in San Pedro from 1978 until his death in 1994. (File photo) 

[Expand](https://www.dailybreeze.com/2019/08/13/bukowski-in-bronze-aims-to-create-san-pedro-monument-to-author/#)

It’s not uncommon for tourists, some from other countries, to wind up in San Pedro “searching for Bukowski,” as it were.

That would be Charles Bukowski, the hard-drinking, underground poet who became a well-known figure in San Pedro in his later years and is buried at nearby Green Hills Memorial Park.

But there are no monuments to the writer who died in 1994. No plaques, no statues. And that leaves some tourists surprised and disappointed. Bukowski moved to San Pedro in 1978 and was a familiar face at area businesses, including the Vinegar Hill Bookstore, Williams Bookstore, the City Fish Market and Sacred Grounds coffee house.

In 2015, the community celebrated [what would have been his 95th birthday](https://www.dailybreeze.com/2015/08/11/san-pedro-tribute-to-celebrate-writer-charles-bukowskis-95th-birthday/) with poetry readings, a screening of “Factotum” — a 2005 adaptation of Bukowski’s 1975 novel of the same name — and a Q&A panel.

Now, plans are quickly being developed for renowned San Pedro sculptor Eugene Daub to create a larger-than-life bronze statue honoring the writer, with a goal of having it ready to unveil on Aug. 16, 2020, which would have been Bukowski’s 100th birthday.

The location is yet to be determined, but would be somewhere on Sixth Street where Bukowski spent so much time.

The idea was spearheaded by Angela Romero of the fledgling San Pedro Heritage Museum project, heard about some recent tourists from Germany who came looking for Bukowski memorabilia in San Pedro. She’d like to see the statue at the plaza area on Sixth and Mesa streets, but no specific location is under discussion officially.

“There’s a kinship between Bukowski and San Pedro,” Romero, a local historian, said.

San Pedro seemed to resonate with Bukowski when he moved from East Hollywood, she said.

“I think it was the distance it gave him from his old life,” Romero said of town’s working waterfront and working-class vibe. “The one thing no one’s been able to bottle is the authenticity that’s here (in San Pedro).”

From the [Daily Breeze’s South Bay History column](http://blogs.dailybreeze.com/history/2010/10/06/charles-bukowski/) on Oct. 6, 2010:

_(Bukowski) populated his writings with loners and drunks carousing in seedy bars, and hardscrabble characters eking out a living on the city’s less-glamorous streets._

_In 1978, he moved from East Hollywood to a quiet neighborhood in San Pedro, where he became an increasingly well-known resident until his death on March 9, 1994. He came to love San Pedro’s blue-collar, unassuming atmosphere, even as his celebrity and stature continued to grow._

A launch party to raise the needed $150,000 for the “Bukowski in Bronze” project will be held at 7 p.m. Friday, Aug. 16, at Sacred Grounds coffee house where Bukowski’s poetry will be read and a birthday cake will be shared on what would have been his 99th birthday.

A [Go FundMe page](https://www.gofundme.com/f/bukowski) also has been set up and the office of Los Angeles City Councilman Joe Buscaino, which is throwing its full support behind the idea, believes the numerous social media pages dedicated to Bukowski — most with a global reach — will bring funding in quickly.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VjrC1bNykYY)

For a project that’s just been announced, there’s already a growing enthusiasm.

What about the rather misogynist bent found in many of his works?

“Bukowski’s not for everyone,” Romero said. “This statue is for his fans and for San Pedro to finally recognize him. He was a great writer.”

Daub already has met with Bukowski’s widow, Linda, who still lives in the house the couple shared, to gather up photographs and ideas.

One thought is to create an interactive piece where fans could sit next to the author and have pictures taken. One early sketch shows Bukowski at his old manual typewriter, a cat — he loved cats — at his feet. But there are other designs being weighed as well.

Daub said after spending time with Bukowski’s wife and going through hundreds of photographs and other memorabilia, he discovered a “warm, personal, kind man.”

On what would have been Harry Bridges’ 118th birthday, a bronze statue depicting the iconic union leader was unveiled Sunday, July 28, in Wilmington.

The [life-sized statue](https://www.dailybreeze.com/2019/05/31/port-union-icon-harry-bridges-being-memorialized-in-life-sized-bronze-statue/), created by sculptor Eugene Daub, stands in front of the doors of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union’s new dispatch hall at Anaheim and Alameda streets.

Organized labor pioneer Bridges founded the union — and remains its most revered figurehead nearly 30 years after his death.

Attending the unveiling were several members of Bridges’ family, including his son, Robbie Bridges, and several grandchildren.

[Video 1](https://www.dailybreeze.com/2019/07/28/monument-to-ilwu-founder-harry-bridges-unveiled-at-unions-dispatch-hall-in-wilmington/)

[Video 2](https://www.dailybreeze.com/2019/07/28/monument-to-ilwu-founder-harry-bridges-unveiled-at-unions-dispatch-hall-in-wilmington/)

Born on July 28, 1901, in Australia, Bridges arrived in San Francisco in 1920 where his subsequent union organizing activities a few years later landed him in jail.

Bridges also was threatened with deportation, but became a naturalized citizen in 1945.

He died on March 30, 1990, at the age of 88.

The statue depicts Bridges speaking at a lectern, his right arm and forefinger extended as he makes a point. The pose was a familiar one of his during his organizing years, according to those who knew Bridges.

The $90,000 statue was commissioned by ILWU’s Southern California Pensioners with strong support by former union President David Arian, who before his death pledged $50,000 toward the cost from the Harry Bridges Foundation.

Greg Mitre, ILWU Pensioner president, and Arian had the idea 10 years ago of creating a monument that would honor the union’s leader and become a “beacon” to workers entering the hall.

Mitre served as host for the outdoor ceremony.

In addition to Daub, the artist, those attending included:

*   ILWU Local 13 President Ray Familathe;
*   ILWU Local 13 Vice President Gary Herrera;
*   ILWU President Willie Adams;
*   Los Angeles County Supervisor Janice Hahn;
*   Los Angeles City Councilmembers Joe Buscaino and Mike Bonin;
*   ILWU Coast Committee member Ponce De Leon;
*   And Los Angeles Harbor Commissioner Diane Middleton.
